title: Small centralizers and their homomorphism amalgamation
statement:
Let $A$ be a nonzero commutative ring and $(G,T=D_A(M))$ a split realization of a finite reduced root datum $(M,\Phi,M^\vee,\Phi^\vee)$ [def-sfb-pinned-split-root-realization]. The root system $\Phi$ admits a base $\Delta$ in that definition. Fix any such base and generators of its free root modules. For $J\subseteq\Delta$, put $L_J=M\cap\operatorname{span}_{\mathbf Q}(J)$ inside $M\otimes_{\mathbf Z}\mathbf Q$, put $S_J=D_A(M/L_J)\subseteq T$ [def-sfb-ring-diagonalizable-group], and let $G_J=Z_G(S_J)$ denote the functor of elements commuting with $S_J$ after every algebra extension. This functor is a closed reductive subgroup containing $T$, and $(G_J,T)$ is a split realization with roots $\Phi_J=\Phi\cap\operatorname{span}_{\mathbf Q}(J)$, their original coroots in $M^\vee$, base $J$, and the inherited simple-root generators. If $I\subseteq J$, there is the natural inclusion $G_I\subseteq G_J$. In particular $G_\varnothing=T$, $G_\Delta=G$, and $G_J$ has semisimple rank $|J|$.

Let $H$ be any affine $A$-group scheme (an affine scheme over $\operatorname{Spec}A$ with multiplication, identity and inverse satisfying the group diagrams). Suppose given homomorphisms $g_J:G_J\to H$ for all $J\subseteq\Delta$ with $|J|\leq2$, such that $g_J|_{G_I}=g_I$ whenever $I\subseteq J$ and $|J|\leq2$. Then there is a unique homomorphism $g:G\to H$ restricting to every $g_J$. These assertions hold over arbitrary, possibly disconnected or nonreduced, $A$, and include $\Delta=\varnothing$.

proof.text: The root system $\Phi$ has a base. The root-datum axioms of [def-sfb-pinned-split-root-realization] give the data of [lem-sfb-crystallographic-positive-base] with $I=\Phi$, $N=M^\vee$, $\alpha$ the inclusion, $\beta:\gamma\mapsto\gamma^\vee$ (injective, being a bijection onto $\Phi^\vee$) and $\sigma_\gamma$ the permutation induced by the reflection of $\gamma$. Since $\Phi$ is finite and $0\notin\Phi$, choose $f\in M^\vee\otimes\mathbf Q$ outside the finitely many hyperplanes $\{f(\gamma)=0\}$ and clear denominators to get an additive $f:M\to\mathbf Z$ nonzero on $\Phi$. Let $D$ be the set of roots $\gamma$ with $f(\gamma)>0$ that are not a sum of two roots with positive $f$-values. That node makes $D$ linearly independent over $\mathbf Z$, hence over $\mathbf Q$. By induction on $f(\gamma)$, every root with $f(\gamma)>0$ is a sum of elements of $D$: otherwise $\gamma=\gamma'+\gamma''$ with $0<f(\gamma'),f(\gamma'')<f(\gamma)$. The reflection of $\gamma$ sends $\gamma$ to $-\gamma$, so $\Phi=-\Phi$ and every root is a nonnegative or nonpositive integral combination of $D$. Thus $D$ is a base in the sense of that definition; $D=\varnothing$ when $\Phi=\varnothing$. From now on $\Delta$ is any fixed base, with fixed generators $X_\alpha$ of the free modules $\mathfrak g_\alpha$, $\alpha\in\Delta$, so that $G$ is a pinned split realization.

source.place: Existence of a base for the root system of a split reductive group, used before Corollary 6.2.7, p.204; standard positive-indecomposable construction (Mathlib RootPairing base existence). Added by the maintainer reader Q132 review.

proof.text: For $J\subseteq\Delta$, $M/L_J$ is finitely generated, and torsion-free: $nm\in L_J$ implies $m\in\operatorname{span}_{\mathbf Q}(J)$ and hence $m\in L_J$. By [lem-trf-fg-torsionfree-group-free] it has a finite integral basis. The group-algebra description [def-sfb-ring-diagonalizable-group] therefore identifies $S_J$ with a product of multiplicative groups. The Hopf map $A[M]\to A[M/L_J]$ is surjective, so the duality statement [lem-sfb-relative-diagonalizable-character-duality] makes it a closed subgroup of $T$. A root $\gamma$ restricts trivially to $S_J$ exactly when its image in $M/L_J$ is zero: compare the basis monomials $e_{\bar\gamma}$ and $e_0$ in the group algebra. This is exactly $\gamma\in\Phi_J$. The base-coordinate definition says a root is in this rational span exactly when every coefficient outside $J$ is zero; consequently its positive or negative integral expansion uses only $J$. Thus $J$ is a base of this subsystem.

source.place: Corollary 6.2.7 setup and Isogeny Theorem Step 1, pp.204--205; explicit saturated-lattice argument. Read online; local archival copy WANTED. No Stacks tag states this reductive-group result.

proof.text:
Apply [lem-sfb-relative-torus-centralizer-normalizer] to the smooth affine finitely presented $G$ and the closed split torus $S_J$ from step 2. This represents $G_J$ as a smooth affine finitely presented closed subgroup, commutes with arbitrary base change, and identifies its Lie algebra with the $S_J$-invariants. Apply [lem-sfb-relative-torus-automorphism-fixed-group] to conjugation by $S_J$ on $G$: the fixed functor is precisely this centralizer, and since $G$ is reductive, so is $G_J$. The commutative torus $T$ lies in $G_J$; it remains maximal on every geometric fibre since a larger torus there would already be a larger torus in $G$. In the prescribed $M$-weight decomposition of $\mathfrak g$, restriction of weights along $M\to M/L_J$ keeps exactly weights in $L_J$, by [lem-sfb-relative-torus-bundle-weights]. Hence
$$\operatorname{Lie}(G_J)=\operatorname{Lie}(T)\oplus\bigoplus_{\gamma\in\Phi_J}\mathfrak g_\gamma.$$
This equality and its base-change compatibility identify the geometric roots, not merely their differentials; all retained root modules remain the given free rank-one modules.

source.place: Lemma 2.2.4, pp.64--66, and torus-centralizer discussion preceding Remark 3.1.5, p.83; Isogeny Theorem Step 1, pp.204--205. Read online; local archival copy WANTED. No Stacks tag states this reductive-group result.

proof.text: By [lem-sfb-split-root-subgroup-weyl-calculus], the root exponentials in the reductive subgroup $G_J$ containing $T$ agree with the original ones, as do their coroots. Together with steps 2--3, this gives precisely the split realization and inherited generators required by [def-sfb-pinned-split-root-realization]. Its root-span dimension is $|J|$ because $J$ is independent and spans $\Phi_J$, so the rank formula in that calculus gives the asserted semisimple rank. If $I\subseteq J$, the quotient $M/L_I\to M/L_J$ shows $S_J\subseteq S_I$, hence commuting with $S_I$ implies commuting with $S_J$ after every extension; this gives the natural subgroup inclusion. Since $L_\varnothing=0$, $S_\varnothing=T$ and the self-centralizing-torus assertion in the calculus gives $G_\varnothing=T$. Every root is trivial on $S_\Delta$, so equivariance of its exponential makes $S_\Delta$ commute with every root group and with $T$. Their generation of $G$ as a sheaf makes it commute with $G$, so $G_\Delta=G$. For $\Delta=\varnothing$ these equalities already give $G=T$; take $g=g_\varnothing$, and uniqueness is immediate.

source.place: Isogeny Theorem Step 1, pp.204--205; Theorem 4.1.4, Corollary 5.1.9 and the open-cell generation of Section 6.2, p.198. Read online; local archival copy WANTED. No Stacks tag states this reductive-group result.

proof.text: Assume $\Delta$ is nonempty. Write $f_T=g_\varnothing$, $f_\alpha=g_{\{\alpha\}}|_{U_\alpha}$ and $h_\alpha=g_{\{\alpha\}}(n_\alpha)$. These expressions are defined: step 4 and [lem-sfb-split-root-subgroup-weyl-calculus] put $U_{\pm\alpha}$ and $n_\alpha$ in $G_{\{\alpha\}}$. For distinct simple roots set $q_{\alpha\beta}=g_{\{\alpha,\beta\}}|_{U_{\Psi_{\alpha\beta}}}$. All roots in $\Psi_{\alpha\beta}$ vanish on $S_{\{\alpha,\beta\}}$, so their root groups lie in that centralizer; their product subgroup does too by the product assertion in the calculus. Compatibility of the given $g_J$ says $q_{\alpha\beta}|_{U_\alpha}=f_\alpha$, $q_{\alpha\beta}|_{U_\beta}=f_\beta$, and gives the common map $f_T$ on $T$. The linked choices in each $G_J$ agree with those in $G$.

source.place: Corollary 6.2.7 deduced from Theorem 6.2.4, p.204; construction of the supplied relation data. Read online; local archival copy WANTED. No Stacks tag states this reductive-group result.

proof.text: Inside $G_{\{\alpha\}}$, apply the homomorphism $g_{\{\alpha\}}$ to the identities of [lem-sfb-split-root-subgroup-weyl-calculus], after an arbitrary $A$-algebra extension. Conjugation by $t$ on $U_\alpha$ gives $f_T(t)f_\alpha(u)f_T(t)^{-1}=f_\alpha(tut^{-1})$; conjugation by $n_\alpha$ on $T$ gives $h_\alpha f_T(t)h_\alpha^{-1}=f_T(s_\alpha(t))$. The square and cubic relations give $h_\alpha^2=f_T(\alpha^\vee(-1))$ and $(h_\alpha f_\alpha(\exp_\alpha(X_\alpha)))^3=1$. Inside $G_{\{\alpha,\beta\}}$, the elements $n_\alpha,n_\beta$ have images $h_\alpha,h_\beta$ by compatibility. Applying this homomorphism to $(n_\alpha n_\beta)^{m_{\alpha\beta}}=t_{\alpha\beta}$ therefore gives $(h_\alpha h_\beta)^{m_{\alpha\beta}}=f_T(t_{\alpha\beta})$. For $c\in\Psi_{\alpha\beta}\setminus\{\alpha\}$, both $u\in U_c$ and $n_\alpha u n_\alpha^{-1}$ lie in $U_{\Psi_{\alpha\beta}}$. Applying the same homomorphism yields $h_\alpha q_{\alpha\beta}(u)h_\alpha^{-1}=q_{\alpha\beta}(n_\alpha u n_\alpha^{-1})$. Interchanging $\alpha,\beta$ gives the other conjugation identity. These are all the hypotheses, including the two distinct rank-two checks, of [lem-sfb-pinned-root-relations-hom-criterion].

source.place: Theorem 6.2.4, relations (6.2.2)--(6.2.6), pp.201--202, checked inside the supplied small centralizers. Read online; local archival copy WANTED. No Stacks tag states this reductive-group result.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-pinned-root-relations-hom-criterion] to the data of steps 5--6 and the given affine $H$. It yields a homomorphism $g:G\to H$ with those torus and simple-root restrictions and the values $h_\alpha$ on $n_\alpha$. For nonempty $J\subseteq\Delta$, $|J|\leq2$, compare $g|_{G_J}$ and $g_J$. They agree on $T$, each simple-root group for $\alpha\in J$, and each $n_\alpha$, by their definitions and compatibility with $g_{\{\alpha\}}$. Step 4 identifies these as the canonical data of the pinned split group $G_J$, so the uniqueness part of the criterion, applied to $G_J$ itself, gives $g|_{G_J}=g_J$. The empty restriction is already $f_T=g_\varnothing$. Finally any other extension has exactly the same torus map, simple-root maps and $n_\alpha$ values, so the same uniqueness assertion for $G$ identifies it with $g$. All equations used are identities on arbitrary algebra-valued points; no argument passes from geometric equality to equality over a possibly nonreduced base.
